chapter.title: Messages to Python Objects
chapter.para: A Python object is used from Rexx with ordinary messages. Most of them are not methods of PyObject: they reach its method, which looks the name up among the Python object's attributes when the message arrives, so an attribute added later is found.

section.title: Attributes and Calls
section.para: The forms of a message, and what each does in Python:

row.entry: Rexx
Python
o.name(a, b): the attribute, called with the arguments
o.name, called with no arguments when it is a function or a method; classes and modules are returned, not called
o.name = v, for an attribute that exists
o(a, b): the object itself, called (a class makes an instance)
o~getattr("name"), o~setattr("name", v), o~invoke("name", a, b)
the same, with the exact name

section.para: Because classes are returned rather than called, np~linalg~det(m) works, and an instance is made with new: .py~import("collections")~Counter~new("abba") is collections.Counter("abba"). The same holds for the builtins: .py~dict is the class dict, and .py~dict~new an empty dict.
Because functions and methods are called, a method cannot be taken as a value with o~name: to pass one as a callback or a thread's target, take it with o~getattr("name").

example.title: Attributes and calls
example.programlisting:
math = .py~import("math") say math~sqrt(2) math~pi math~floor(2.7) np = .py~import("numpy") say np~linalg~det(np~eye(2)) -- a module's attribute, then a call c = .py~import("collections")~Counter~new("abracadabra") say c~most_common(2)
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Names in Any Case
section.para: ooRexx uppercases message names, and Python's names are case-sensitive, so a name is looked up without regard to case among the object's attributes:

listitem.para: if one attribute matches, it is the one;
otherwise the error names the candidates.

section.para: The exact forms getattr, setattr and invoke take the name as written. They are named as Python's own functions because o["name"] must stay Python's indexing.

example.title: Names in any case, and the exact form
example.programlisting:
logging = .py~import("logging") say logging~getattr("INFO") -- the constant: logging~INFO is logging.info say logging~getLevelName(20)
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Items and Slices
section.para: o[k] and o[k] = v are Python's indexing: d["key"], l[0], l[-1]. Several indexes are a tuple, as numpy wants it: m[0, 1] is m[(0, 1)]. Positions count from 0, as in Python, because it is Python's object; gives a sequence as a Rexx Array counting from 1.
A slice is made with Python's builtin slice: o[.py~slice(a, b, step)] is o[a:b:step], with &nil; leaving a part out: x[.py~slice(-3, .nil)] is x[-3:].

example.title: Items and slices
example.programlisting:
d = .py~dict~new d["one"] = 1; d[2] = "two" say d d["one"] d[2] m = .py~import("numpy")~arange(6)~reshape(2, 3) say m[1, 2] m[0] l = .py~list(.py~range(10)) say l[.py~slice(2, 5)] l[.py~slice(.nil, .nil, -3)] l[-1]
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Keyword Arguments
section.para: Keyword arguments go in a marker, a , as the last argument of a call. makes it from names and values, or from a Directory or StringTable: plt~plot(x, y, .py~kw("color", "red", "linewidth", 2)). Only the marker is taken as keywords: a Directory or StringTable at the end of the arguments stays a positional argument. The names go as written, in their case.

example.title: Keyword arguments
example.programlisting:
json = .py~import("json") data = .py~dict~new(.py~kw("b", 1, "a", 2)) say json~dumps(data, .py~kw("sort_keys", .true)) options = .directory~new options["sep"] = "-" show = .py~eval("lambda *a, **k: (a, k)") say show~new(1, .py~kw(options)) -- a Directory made into keywords say show~new(1, options)~class~id -- a Directory as itself
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Operators, Comparisons and Iteration
section.para: Rexx's operators on a PyObject are Python's, so that Python numbers, sets and numpy arrays work in Rexx expressions. The left operand must be the Python object, because Rexx sends the operator to it; with a Rexx value on the left, the operation is Rexx's own, on the Python object's string value.

row.entry: Rexx
Python
a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b, a ** b
a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b, a ** b
a % b (integer division)
a // b (remainder)
-a, +a, not a
a < b, a > b, a <= b, a >= b
a < b, a > b, a <= b, a >= b
a = b, a \= b (also <>, ><)
a == b, a != b
a == b, a \== b
a is b, a is not b
a & b, a | b, a && b
a & b, a | b, a ^ b
say o, o~string
consistent with == (identity), so that a PyObject can be the index of a Rexx collection

section.para: Note the two divisions: Rexx's % is integer division and // the remainder, Python's // and %. The meaning is kept, not the symbol.

example.title: Operators and iteration
example.programlisting:
a = .py~int(7); b = .py~int(2) say a + b a - b a * b a / b a % b a // b a ** b (-a) say (a < b) (a = .py~int(7)) (a \= b) l = .py~list((1, 2)); m = .py~list((1, 2)) say (l = m) (l == m) -- equal, but not the same object s = .py~set((1, 2)); t = .py~set((2, 3)) say (s & t) (s | t) (s && t) do x over .py~range(3); say x; end
::requires "python.cls"

section.title: Methods of the Object Class
section.para: A PyObject is a Rexx object, so the methods of Rexx's Object class are Rexx's: class, isA, string, hasMethod, objectName and the others. l~class is the class PyObject; Python's class is l~getattr("__class__"), or .py~type(l).

Five are the exception, because Python objects commonly have them too: copy (dict.copy), send (a generator's), start and run (threading.Thread's) and request without arguments (the request of a socketserver handler) are Python's when the object has that attribute, and Rexx's otherwise. See .
